title: Add command line option for doing POSTs

judge.reasoning: Both patches add an option to fetch, view (via fetch), shell and parse, but Patch A delivers what the issue asks for: a `--data` option that behaves like `curl -d` (POST by default, body set, `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`), plus `-X/--method` to override the method. The independent tests confirm it: A passes all five scenarios, while B fails the form-encoding check because `Request.from_curl` does not add the Content-Type header that real `curl -d` sends, so servers expecting form data may not parse B's POST body. B's `--curl COMMAND` design is a reasonable, more general alternative, but it forces users to embed a whole curl command string rather than offering the simple data flag the issue requests, and its parse-command test does not exercise a POST at all. A's tests cover each command (fetch, parse, shell, view, including the reactorless shell path and the method/data interaction and empty-method validation); the view test is skipped only on Windows, which is a reasonable constraint for a fake-browser script and still runs on the platforms the issue implies. On craft, A adds a news entry and consistent docs for every command; B imports `SequenceExclude` from `scrapy.utils.datatypes` while the neighbouring fetch command uses `scrapy.utils._datatypes`, suggesting a deprecated import path, and changes the `set_spidercls` signature of the parse command. B's usage-error handling and URL/curl exclusivity checks are fine but do not outweigh the functional gap. A is the better fix.

issue_md:
Previously reported by pablo on Trac http://dev.scrapy.org/ticket/292

It would be nice to add a command line option for performing POSTs, like curl -d does.

This would be added to all commands that accepts a url argument, like crawl, parse, shell, fetch and view.

title: Adding support to FTP file listing

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make a trailing-slash FTP URL perform a listing, and both pass all four independent tests. The differences are in what the listing is and how edges are handled.

Correctness: Patch A issues the FTP LIST command (via twisted's FTPFileListProtocol) and returns a JSON array of structured entries including filetype, size, and name. That matches the issue's wording ('calls FTP list') and actually enables the stated goal of scanning repositories, since a crawler needs to know which entries are directories to recurse. Patch B uses NLST, returning bare names one per line, which gives no way to distinguish files from subdirectories. Patch A also preserves the existing error semantics: a nonexistent directory raises CommandFailed and maps to a 404 like a nonexistent file does. Patch B's own test codifies that a nonexistent directory returns 200 with an empty body, indistinguishable from an empty directory, which is a regression in error reporting relative to the handler's existing conventions. Patch A also keeps ftp_local_filename working for listings and sets the response class to JsonResponse only when the body is the listing itself. Patch B does handle an empty path (ftp://host with no slash) where A would still call retrieveFile(''), a small point in B's favor.

Tests: Patch A adds four tests covering root listing (names, sizes, filetypes, headers), subdirectory listing with a quoted space in the path, nonexistent directory -> 404, and the local-filename path, and extends both fixture trees with a subdirectory so the dir/file distinction is exercised. Patch B adds two tests: root listing names only, and the nonexistent-directory-returns-200-empty behavior, which locks in the weaker semantics.

Scope/craft: Both update the docs. Patch A also updates the module docstring that describes the handler's response shape; B leaves it stale. A's local import inside the helper is slightly unusual but harmless. A's reliance on Unix ls-style LIST parsing is a portability caveat, but NLST's lack of type information is the bigger practical gap for the issue's goal.

Overall A resolves the issue more completely, with better error handling and substantially stronger tests.

title: Image pipeline should allow to decide whether to auto-convert to jpg or not

judge.reasoning: Both patches add an opt-out setting and both pass the independent tests, so the difference lies in correctness at the edges, compatibility, and craft. Patch A changes the signature of `convert_image` to require a new keyword-only `image_format` argument with no default or deprecation path; any subclass that overrides `convert_image` with the old signature will raise TypeError when the base pipeline calls it, and A had to rewrite existing tests to match (the 5 removed test lines). Patch B leaves `convert_image` untouched and routes the no-convert case through a separate helper, so existing overrides keep working. On behaviour, A stores preserved-format files with no extension at all, while B reuses the FilesPipeline URL-extension logic (`.png`, `.gif`, etc.), which is more useful and consistent with the sibling pipeline. B also handles the MPO-opened-JPEG case, wraps unsupported-format thumbnail saves in ImageException with a clear message, and falls back to application/octet-stream for unknown MIME types; A has an unguarded `assert orig_image.format is not None` and would surface raw Pillow errors for formats that can't be saved. B's extra change to `_key_for_pipe` is scope beyond the issue, but it is directly motivated: without it a class-prefixed `*_IMAGES_CONVERT_TO_JPEG = False` would be silently ignored, and it is covered by a dedicated test; the risk is small since callers only use the returned key with a default. Tests: A covers file_path, convert_image, and image_downloaded for the new mode; B covers those plus the default content-type, min-size check in the new path, the custom-settings matrix, and the class-attr vs setting override, with end-to-end on-disk verification. Docs are comparable; B adds a news entry and versionadded. Overall B resolves the issue without breaking the existing API and with better edge handling.

+
+Keeping the original image format
+---------------------------------
+
+.. setting:: IMAGES_CONVERT_TO_JPEG
+
+.. versionadded:: VERSION
+
+By default, the Images Pipeline converts all downloaded images, and their
+thumbnails, to JPEG images in RGB mode, and stores them with a ``.jpg``
+extension.
+
+To store images exactly as downloaded instead, set
+:setting:`IMAGES_CONVERT_TO_JPEG` to ``False``:
+

+
+When this setting is ``False``:
+
+* The full image is stored with the same bytes it was downloaded with.
+
+* Thumbnails are saved in the format of the original image (e.g. PNG
+  thumbnails for PNG images).
+
+* The file extension of both the full image and its thumbnails is determined
+  from the image URL, the same way as for the :ref:`Files Pipeline
+  <topics-file-naming>` (it may be empty if it cannot be determined).
+
+* The ``Content-Type`` sent to storage backends that support it (e.g. Amazon S3
+  or Google Cloud Storage) matches the format of the original image.

title: RetryMiddleware doesn't actually retry HttpCompressionMiddleware errors

judge.reasoning:
The issue asks that decompression failures in HttpCompressionMiddleware actually get retried, as the RETRY_EXCEPTIONS comment promises. Patch A delivers that under default settings: it catches the decompression error family in process_response and calls get_retry_request, honoring RETRY_ENABLED, RETRY_TIMES, dont_retry, max_retry_times, priority_adjust and give_up_log_level, and re-raises once retries are exhausted. The independent tests confirm it: all three fail on base and pass on A. Its tests are substantive (parametrized over gzip/deflate/br/zstd, exhausted-retry, dont_retry, RETRY_ENABLED=False, and a no-retry check for the max-size IgnoreRequest path), and the manager-level test shows a Request coming out of the full middleware chain. Weaknesses: it duplicates retry policy inside the compression middleware rather than routing through RetryMiddleware, ignores RETRY_EXCEPTIONS, and will retry even if RetryMiddleware itself is removed from DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARES. Those are design compromises, not failures to fix the issue.

Patch B attacks the root cause more structurally (exceptions from process_response reach the remaining process_exception methods, plus a new DecompressionError in RETRY_EXCEPTIONS), but gates the fix behind a new setting DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARE_RESPONSE_EXCEPTIONS that defaults to False. With defaults, nothing is retried; the independent tests fail on B exactly as on base, just with a renamed exception. Its own manager-level default test still asserts the failure propagates. So for existing projects the reported bug remains, and users who relied on catching OSError/BadGzipFile in errbacks now get a different exception type. B also carries significant unrelated churn and risk: it rewrites DownloaderMiddlewareManager to store None placeholders in the method deques, adds CloseSpider handling in the scraper and downloader manager with its own crawl tests, emits a deprecation warning on every process_response exception (including IgnoreRequest raised to drop a response) when any user process_exception exists, and changes the project template. None of that is needed to make retries work, and it widens the blast radius of the change.

On correctness for the scenario the issue describes, A resolves it and B does not by default; A's tests are stronger for the issue's behavior; B's scope expansion adds risk. A wins.

A comment in the code of RetryMiddleware says

```
    # IOError is raised by the HttpCompression middleware when trying to
    # decompress an empty response
```

when including IOError in the exceptions to retry.

But IOError would be raised in HttpCompressionMiddleware's `process_response()`, errors from which are not handled by `process_exception()` in downloader middlewares.

title: get_project_settings of doesn't reflect per-spider settings

judge.reasoning: The issue is a user misunderstanding with two components: get_project_settings() is documented nowhere and does not include spider settings, and custom_settings assigned in __init__ is silently ignored because spider settings are read from the class before instantiation. Patch A only adds a docstring and a brief docs mention of get_project_settings; it does nothing about the silent-ignore half, which is what actually confused the reporter, and adds no tests. Patch B documents both points explicitly (a note in settings.rst stating custom_settings must be a class attribute and that get_project_settings excludes spider settings, plus a fuller docstring), and adds a targeted runtime UserWarning in Crawler._create_spider when custom_settings is found on the instance and differs from the class attribute. The check is narrow and low-risk (vars() membership plus identity comparison), covers both the __init__ case and the spider-argument case, and points users at the correct alternatives (class attribute, update_settings, from_crawler with priority='spider'). It is backed by four tests that would fail before the change and pass after, including a full crawl_async run. The independent evidence confirms this: only Patch B passes the 'not silently ignored' test, while the 'override in __init__' test fails on both since neither (correctly) changes the settings model. The warning is a modest behavior addition beyond pure docs, but it directly targets the reported confusion rather than being unrelated churn. B is the more complete and better-verified fix.

title: Raising CloseSpider from DownloaderMiddleware doesn't work

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause identically: in Scraper.handle_downloader_output_async, a CloseSpider carried by the download Failure is now routed to engine.close_spider_async instead of to the request errback / 'Error downloading' log. The independent tests confirm both pass every scenario (process_request, process_response, async process_response, no reason, high-priority middleware). The difference is scope and risk. Patch A stays on the issue: a small scraper change factored into a `_close_spider_on_exception` helper reused by handle_spider_error, a docstring update, and a targeted robotstxt change so a CloseSpider raised while downloading robots.txt is re-raised instead of being swallowed by the generic `except Exception` (a real way the issue's symptom could persist). Its tests cover process_request, process_response, process_exception, the no-reason default, and the robots.txt path, and assert the spider stops early and nothing is logged as an error. Patch B bundles the same one-hunk fix with a large unrelated feature: a new DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARE_RESPONSE_EXCEPTIONS setting, rewritten process_response/process_exception chaining with None placeholders in the method deques, a changed `_process_exception` return type, a new DecompressionError, RETRY_EXCEPTIONS edits, a project-template default flip, and a deprecation warning that fires for any user middleware raising from process_response (including IgnoreRequest) when another user middleware defines process_exception. It also silently changes existing behaviour by no longer passing CloseSpider from process_request to process_exception methods. None of this is asked for by the issue, it buries the fix in ~600 lines of diff, and it introduces real behavioural risk for users. B's issue-specific tests are thinner than A's (two cases, no process_exception or no-reason case). On correctness the patches tie; on tests A is somewhat stronger; on scope B is clearly worse; on craft A's helper extraction is cleaner. A wins.

title: Scrapy capitalizes headers for request

judge.reasoning: The issue is that lowercase request header names arrive at the server Title-Cased when using Scrapy's default (HTTP11, Twisted-based) download handler, including through an HTTP proxy. Patch B fixes exactly that path: it records each header's original spelling in Headers (keeping the stored keys Title-Case for backward compatibility), exposes original_case_items(), and wraps Twisted's Headers in a _CasePreservingTxHeaders whose getAllRawHeaders() emits the original names, with copy() and removeHeader() overridden so the Agent's internal header copy and the tunneling agent's Proxy-Authorization removal keep working. It also propagates original case to to_dict/request_from_dict, request_to_curl, to_tuple_list/to_unicode_dict, copy and pickling. The independent tests confirm it: all five pass, including the default-handler and proxy on-the-wire checks that fail on base. Patch B's own tests use a raw socket server to assert the actual bytes sent, both direct and via proxy; the skip for secure/http2 is a test-infrastructure limitation and the same TxHeaders code path serves HTTPS, so the fix covers the issue's https URL. Patch A changes Headers.normkey to preserve the first-seen spelling, which fixes to_tuple_list and the aiohttp/httpx handlers, but it never touches the HTTP11 handler, which still builds a plain TxHeaders that Twisted canonicalizes to Title-Case. The three default-handler independent tests still FAIL-ASSERT on Patch A, and Patch A's own docs table admits HTTP11 remains 'Capitalized', so the reported scenario stays broken. Patch A also makes normkey O(n) on every lookup and changes the observable keys() of both request and response Headers (e.g. httpx response headers now in raw server case), a wider behavioral change than the ask with no benefit for the default handler. B resolves the root cause at the wire for the handler the issue describes and has stronger tests; A masks only the in-memory representation.

I'm setting the headers following way
```python
headers = {
    'accept': 'text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/webp,*/*;q=0.8',
```

And calling request like that:
```
yield scrapy.Request(url='https:/myurl.com/', callback=self.parse, headers=headers, cookies=cookies, meta={'proxy': 'http://localhost:8888'})
```
And it makes that scrapy capitalizes all these headers and it looks like that (I'm using Charles proxy for debugging):
```
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/webp,*/*;q=0.8
Cache-Control: no-cache
```
And this is not working correctly for my case.

If I'm using curl and set headers lowercase
```
accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/webp,*/*;q=0.8
cache-control: no-cache
```
everything works like a charm.

Is there any way how I can disable this capitalizing behavior in Scrapy?
Thanks for any help!

+    """Run a plain HTTP server that records the raw bytes of the request

+                if not chunk:

+                data += chunk

+    thread.start()
+    try:

+    finally:

title: Can't get partial response body after timeout

judge.reasoning: Patch A's change to scrapy/core/downloader/handlers/http11.py adds `if not isinstance(result, Failure)` without importing `Failure`, so every timeout on the default HTTP/1.1 handler now raises NameError. The independent tests confirm this: on Patch A, not only do the partial-response tests still fail, but the default-behaviour test (data loss not allowed, timeout should raise DownloadTimeoutError) regresses from PASS on base to FAIL with NameError. That is a hard breakage of the most common code path. Patch A also skips its own new HTTP test for handlers that don't opt in and only works for aiohttp. Patch B passes all independent tests across http11 (HTTP and HTTPS), aiohttp, the crawl-level scenarios, and the default-behaviour test. Its design is sound: it keeps the reader reference in _ScrapyAgent and returns the buffered body flagged as dataloss from _cb_timeout only when headers were received and data loss is allowed; otherwise it still raises DownloadTimeoutError. It also extends the behaviour to the HTTP/2 stream, uses the broader httpx.TimeoutException and aioftp's timeout exception set, adds tests for both meta and setting paths plus the no-headers case and FTP, and documents the behaviour in settings.rst. B is strictly better on correctness, tests, and craft.

issue_md:
I'm working on scraping some pages that hold the HTTP connection open indefinitely, trickling data to the client little by little.  I had hoped to use a short timeout to grab the page up to a certain point, but after the timeout is triggered, I can't get at the data that was received.  I thought that setting DOWNLOAD_FAIL_ON_DATALOSS=False would allow partial responses to be processed, but I still get `twisted.internet.error.TimeoutError: User timeout caused connection failure`.  If I use `errback=` on the request, the errback just gets the TimeoutError object and not the response.

Should setting DOWNLOAD_FAIL_ON_DATALOSS=True allow timed out responses to be processed?  Or is there another way to deal with partial responses after a timeout?

title: --pdb catches some harmless internal exceptions

judge.reasoning:
Both patches remove `failure.startDebugMode()` (the root cause: it breaks into pdb on every Failure construction, including the handled OpenSSL SysCallError from the issue) and replace it with a hook that only fires for reported errors. Both pass the independent tests for the issue's exact scenario (handled SSL error, successful crawl, real spider error still debugged).

Correctness differences: Patch B only hooks Python logging records at ERROR with exc_info. Twisted-reported errors (notably 'Unhandled error in Deferred', which the Scrapy log shows at ERROR via the PythonLoggingObserver bridge that carries no exc_info) will no longer enter the debugger under B, a regression versus base for a class of real errors. Patch A additionally observes Twisted's log for isError events with a Failure, catches exceptions that propagate out of the command (excluding UsageError), dedups so the same exception is debugged once even if logged by several components, and guards against fake `_Traceback` objects from cleaned Failures (B would hand such an object to pdb.post_mortem). A also keeps tracebacks through `Failure.cleanFailure` so late-logged failures remain debuggable. That monkeypatch is invasive, but it is scoped to --pdb, context-managed, and restored; B instead leaves its handler on the root logger permanently.

The one independent test A failed did so because A entered the debugger for a different, genuinely reported error ('[Errno 98] Address already in use', Twisted-logged in that environment), not for the handled 'harmless' Deferred error the test targets. A's code produces no log or observer event for an errback-consumed failure, and A's own unit and subprocess tests cover exactly that case, so this result does not show A leaving the issue broken; it reflects A's broader (and consistent with the issue's criterion: debug only what is reported as an error) coverage.

Tests: A adds unit tests for every path (handled failure not debugged, logged error debugged once, warning not debugged, cleaned failure, Twisted log.err, unhandled Deferred, propagated exception, UsageError, patch restoration) plus subprocess tests asserting the debugger is entered exactly once for reported errors and never for handled ones, and asserts startDebugMode is never called. B's subprocess tests are reasonable but thinner (one asserts only that '(Pdb)' appears, without checking exit status) and do not cover Twisted-reported errors.

B is admirably minimal, but A resolves the issue while preserving the debugger for all reported errors and is better tested; the extra machinery is justified and well-explained.

+"""Post-mortem debugging support for the ``--pdb`` command-line option.
+
+Twisted's own debug mode (:func:`twisted.python.failure.startDebugMode`)
+enters the debugger whenever a :class:`~twisted.python.failure.Failure` is
+created from an exception, including exceptions that are later handled
+(e.g. ``OpenSSL.SSL.SysCallError`` raised by Twisted's TLS code when a server
+closes the connection). Instead, the debugger is only entered for errors that
+are actually reported: errors logged with a traceback at ``ERROR`` level or
+higher, errors logged by Twisted (e.g. unhandled errors in Deferreds) and
+exceptions that propagate out of the command.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import gc
+import logging
+import sys
+from contextlib import contextmanager
+from types import TracebackType
+from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any
+
+from twisted.python import log as twisted_log
+from twisted.python.failure import Failure
+
+from scrapy.exceptions import UsageError
+
+if TYPE_CHECKING:
+    from collections.abc import Callable, Iterator
+
+
+class _PostMortemDebugger:
+    def __init__(self) -> None:
+        # Exceptions already debugged, so that an exception reported more than
+        # once (e.g. by different components) only enters the debugger once.
+        self._debugged: list[BaseException] = []
+
+    def debug(self, exc_value: BaseException | None, tb: Any) -> None:
+        # Fake tracebacks (e.g. from cleaned Failures) cannot be debugged.
+        if exc_value is None or not isinstance(tb, TracebackType):
+            return
+        if any(debugged is exc_value for debugged in self._debugged):
+            return
+        self._debugged.append(exc_value)
+        try:
+            strrepr = str(exc_value)
+        except Exception:
+            strrepr = "broken str"
+        print(f"Jumping into debugger for post-mortem of exception {strrepr!r}:")
+        # Imported here so that ipdb is used if it was installed as "pdb".
+        import pdb  # noqa: T100,PLC0415
+
+        pdb.post_mortem(tb)
+
+    def debug_failure(self, failure: Failure) -> None:
+        self.debug(failure.value, failure.tb)
+
+
+class _PostMortemLogHandler(logging.Handler):
+    def __init__(self, debugger: _PostMortemDebugger):
+        super().__init__(logging.ERROR)
+        self._debugger = debugger
+
+    def emit(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> None:
+        if record.exc_info:
+            self._debugger.debug(record.exc_info[1], record.exc_info[2])
+
+
+def _keep_traceback(
+    clean_failure: Callable[[Failure], None],
+) -> Callable[[Failure], None]:
+    """Wrap :meth:`Failure.cleanFailure` so that it keeps the traceback.
+
+    Older Twisted versions clean the failures that reach the end of a
+    Deferred callback chain, dropping their traceback before they are
+    logged."""
+
+    def cleanFailure(self: Failure) -> None:
+        tb = self.tb
+        value = self.value
+        value_tb = getattr(value, "__traceback__", None)
+        clean_failure(self)
+        self.tb = tb
+        if value is not None and value_tb is not None:
+            value.__traceback__ = value_tb
+
+    return cleanFailure
+
+
+@contextmanager
+def post_mortem_on_error() -> Iterator[None]:
+    """Enter the post-mortem debugger for errors reported within the
+    context."""
+    debugger = _PostMortemDebugger()
+
+    def twisted_observer(event: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
+        failure = event.get("failure")
+        if event.get("isError") and isinstance(failure, Failure):
+            debugger.debug_failure(failure)
+
+    handler = _PostMortemLogHandler(debugger)
+    original_clean_failure = Failure.cleanFailure
+    Failure.cleanFailure = _keep_traceback(original_clean_failure)  # type: ignore[method-assign]
+    logging.root.addHandler(handler)
+    twisted_log.addObserver(twisted_observer)
+    try:
+        try:
+            yield
+        finally:
+            # Report unhandled errors of Deferreds that are not referenced
+            # anymore while the debugger is still enabled.
+            gc.collect()
+    except UsageError:
+        raise
+    except Exception:
+        debugger.debug(*sys.exc_info()[1:])
+        raise
+    finally:
+        twisted_log.removeObserver(twisted_observer)
+        logging.root.removeHandler(handler)
+        Failure.cleanFailure = original_clean_failure  # type: ignore[method-assign]

title: request.meta['download_slot'] is not documented

judge.reasoning: Both patches add a `.. reqmeta:: download_slot` target so the existing list entry resolves, and both independent tests pass on each. Patch A puts the documentation exactly where the issue points: a dedicated download_slot section in the Request.meta special keys part of request-response.rst, explaining what the key holds, how the downloader assigns and populates it, which settings it interacts with, and an example of setting it. It adds small cross-links from the autothrottle and DOWNLOAD_SLOTS docs, and ships a test file that fails on base and passes after (the skip condition only triggers when the docs directory is absent, which does not apply to the scenario). Patch B places the target in settings.rst under DOWNLOAD_SLOTS, so a reader of the special keys list is bounced to the settings page rather than finding the key documented in the section the issue names; the explanation is adequate but less complete than A's. More importantly, B bundles large unrelated churn: documenting roughly ten other meta keys, reordering the list, and a source change in scrapy/http/cookies.py that removes support for the `is_unverifiable` meta key and deletes its test. That is a backward-incompatible behavior change with no connection to the issue, adding risk and obscuring the fix, and B adds no test for the actual reported problem. On correctness both resolve the issue, but A is more precisely targeted, better tested, and free of risky scope creep.

@@ -0,0 +1,63 @@
+"""Check that every Request.meta special key referenced in the docs is
+documented."""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import re
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import pytest
+
+ROOT = Path(__file__).parent.parent
+DOCS_DIR = ROOT / "docs"
+SOURCE_DIR = ROOT / "scrapy"
+
+REFERENCE_RE = re.compile(r":reqmeta:`([^`<]+?)(?:\s*<([^>]+)>)?`")
+DEFINITION_RE = re.compile(r"^\s*\.\. reqmeta:: (\S+)\s*$", re.MULTILINE)
+
+pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(
+    not DOCS_DIR.is_dir(), reason="The docs directory is not available"
+)
+
+
+def _doc_sources() -> list[Path]:
+    return [*DOCS_DIR.rglob("*.rst"), *SOURCE_DIR.rglob("*.py")]
+
+
+def _defined_reqmeta_keys() -> set[str]:
+    keys: set[str] = set()
+    for path in _doc_sources():
+        keys.update(DEFINITION_RE.findall(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")))
+    return keys
+
+
+def _special_keys_list() -> list[str]:
+    text = (DOCS_DIR / "topics" / "request-response.rst").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+    section = text.split("Request.meta special keys", 1)[1]
+    return [
+        match.group(2) or match.group(1)
+        for match in REFERENCE_RE.finditer(section.split("\n.. reqmeta::", 1)[0])
+    ]
+
+
+def test_download_slot_is_documented():
+    assert "download_slot" in _defined_reqmeta_keys()
+    assert "download_slot" in _special_keys_list()
+
+
+def test_special_keys_list_is_documented():
+    missing = sorted(set(_special_keys_list()) - _defined_reqmeta_keys())
+    assert not missing, f"Request.meta special keys without documentation: {missing}"
+
+
+def test_all_reqmeta_references_are_documented():
+    defined = _defined_reqmeta_keys()
+    missing: list[str] = []
+    for path in _doc_sources():
+        text = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        for match in REFERENCE_RE.finditer(text):
+            key = (match.group(2) or match.group(1)).strip()
+            if key not in defined:
+                line = text.count("\n", 0, match.start()) + 1
+                missing.append(f"{path.relative_to(ROOT)}:{line}: {key}")
+    assert not missing, "Undocumented :reqmeta: references:\n" + "\n".join(missing)

title: RFC2616 cache policy checks max-age against wrong date after revalidation

judge.reasoning: The issue names three defects: Age header computed in the wrong time base, no freshening of the stored response on 304, and the unreachable/incorrect `or now` default in `_compute_current_age`. Patch A addresses all three. It exposes the storage timestamp (DBM `<key>_time`, filesystem `timestamp` metadata, with an mtime fallback for old entries) to the policy, rewrites `_compute_current_age` per RFC 7234 4.2.3 as apparent age plus Age header plus resident time, drops the `or now` default, and freshens the cached response on 304 by replacing headers, dropping 1xx Warnings, keeping 2xx, skipping hop-by-hop/Content-Length fields, refusing to freshen on an ETag mismatch, and re-storing with an updated cache time. Patch B only implements the 304 header merge (in-place mutation of the cached response), which makes the headline max-age=60 scenario pass because the 304's Date header is copied over, but leaves the Age header handling and the `now` fallback untouched. The independent tests confirm this: A passes all 12, while B fails the four Age-header tests on both storage backends with the same assertion failures as base, so B leaves part of the reported root cause broken. On tests, A adds five targeted tests with a frozen clock covering revalidation, Age relative to reception time, invalid Date fallback, header freshening, and ETag mismatch; B adds one test for Date/Warning refresh only. On scope, A's extra breadth is exactly what the issue asks for and it also updates the docs; B is narrower than the ask. On craft, A returns a copy rather than mutating the stored object and handles the stale Age header after freshening, which B does not (a leftover Age on the cached response would still be counted against the new Date). A is the better fix.

issue_md:
# Expected behavior

A `Cache-Control: max-age=60` request header should prevent requests to the same URL from being sent more frequently than once per minute. If spiders generate requests for that URL more often, then they should be satisfied from the cache without contacting the origin server.

(For simplicity, I'm assuming that either the origin server hasn't set a shorter `max-age` and hasn't made the response uncacheable, or `HTTPCACHE_IGNORE_RESPONSE_CACHE_CONTROLS` and `HTTPCACHE_ALWAYS_STORE` are set to ignore those restrictions.)

# Actual behavior

The header prevents sending requests for the first minute, but after that every request results in contacting the origin server for revalidation.

# Root cause

RFC 7234 says:

> A response's age is the time that has passed since it was generated by, or successfully validated with, the origin server.

`RFC2616Policy._compute_current_age` computes the wrong age when an `Age` header is present or after at least one 304 response has been received.

As a result, scrapy does not correctly interpret the `Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>` request header.

# Proposed fixes

## Fix handling of `Age` response header

`RFC2616Policy._compute_current_age` is computing results in one of two different time-bases, depending on whether the `Age` header is present. Without the `Age` header, it returns age relative to now. However the `Age` header only provides age relative to when the response was received, which will usually be quite different.

Fixing this requires finding out when the response was stored in the cache. Since the existing cache storage implementations maintain a `timestamp` or `<key>_time` metadata field, existing caches already have that information; it just isn't currently exposed to the cache policy.

## Freshen cached response on successful validation

The `RFC2616Policy` implementations of `should_cache_response` and `is_cached_response_valid` ensure that a 304 response never affects what the spider sees or the cache contents. However, that violates the requirements of [RFC 7234 4.3.4](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7234#section-4.3.4):

> When a cache receives a 304 (Not Modified) response and already has one or more stored 200 (OK) responses for the same cache key, the cache needs to identify which of the stored responses are updated by this new response and then update the stored response(s) with the new information provided in the 304 response.

Since scrapy only keeps one version of the response, and used that version to generate its conditional `GET` request, identifying which one to update is trivial. Then, 

> ...the cache MUST:
>
> -  delete any Warning header fields in the stored response with warn-code 1xx (see Section 5.5);
>
> -  retain any Warning header fields in the stored response with warn-code 2xx; and,
>
> -  use other header fields provided in the 304 (Not Modified) response to replace all instances of the corresponding header fields in the stored response.

In addition, since we need to use the response timestamp to compute the age of the response, that has to get updated to the current time as well. (This has the nice side benefit that the DBM and LevelDB storage backends won't expire responses which have been successfully validated recently.)

## Inappropriate use of `now`

`RFC2616Policy._compute_current_age` shouldn't use `now` as a default date (in `... .get(b'Date')) or now`) because that method is invoked long after the initial request was submitted, when the cached response is being checked for usability for a later request. `now` just isn't a meaningful substitute for the timestamp when the response was generated; the age computation can only be correct if there's a `Date` header in the response.

Fortunately, `HttpCacheMiddleware.process_response` already adds a `Date` header if one is not present, and does so before calling `self.storage.store_response`, so we can rely on it being present in all cached responses.

So the `or now` should just get dropped because it's unreachable, and even if it was reachable, it's also wrong.

(However, I'd think setting a default `Date` header shouldn't rely on enabling the cache middleware. If this were done somewhere globally, I think that would resolve #2221.)

title: RFC: Allow usage of file descriptors or stdin with runspider

judge.reasoning: Both patches make `/dev/fd/N` process-substitution paths and extensionless FIFOs work, and the independent tests confirm that for both. The issue explicitly names a second use case, `-` for stdin, which Patch A implements (reads sys.stdin.buffer, executes as a module named `<stdin>` for tracebacks) and Patch B does not: with B, `runspider -` still hits the `Path('-').exists()` check and fails, as the independent stdin test shows (PASS for A, FAIL-ASSERT for B). On root cause, A distinguishes regular files (still imported with the extension check) from non-regular files (read and exec'd), which is a direct answer to the issue's concern without loosening validation for ordinary files. B instead relaxes the extension check to 'any extension or none' and swaps `import_module` for a bare `SourceFileLoader.exec_module`, which also drops the sys.modules registration the old path had and gives modules names like `63`; it works but is a less targeted change with a small regression surface. On tests, A adds tests for stdin success, stdin no-spider, stdin unable-to-load, stdin traceback filename, /dev/fd pipe, and a named FIFO, with skips only on platforms lacking /dev/fd or mkfifo (the issue's scenarios are POSIX shells, so the skips would not hold there). B adds a single bash process-substitution test. A also documents the new behavior in commands.rst and the command's long description. One uncertainty for A is that its tests rely on `proc` accepting `input=` and `pass_fds=`, which I cannot verify here, but the independent runs show A's production code covers every scenario the issue names, while B leaves the stdin case unaddressed.

https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/004b40a7193a7c0c5138abe764cad6d1d9a4fc57/scrapy/commands/runspider.py#L14

If this check could be improved, more creative uses of `runspider` would be admitted. For example, using a file descriptor avoids creating a temporary file (following example taken from the home page):

```shell
$ pip install scrapy
$ scrapy runspider <(echo <<EOF)
import scrapy

class BlogSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = 'blogspider'
    start_urls = ['https://blog.scrapinghub.com']

    def parse(self, response):
        for title in response.css('.post-header>h2'):
            yield {'title': title.css('a ::text').get()}

        for next_page in response.css('a.next-posts-link'):
            yield response.follow(next_page, self.parse)
EOF
```

Currently, this raises an error because the filename ends up being something like `/dev/fd/324`. Perhaps the extension check could be removed entirely?

Another use case would be to use `-` for `stdin`.

title: H2DownloadHandler: bytes_received signal

judge.reasoning: Both patches thread the crawler down to the Stream and send bytes_received/headers_received via check_stop_download, handle the HEADERS/DATA-with-END_STREAM case by tolerating StreamClosedError on reset, and build the partial response via make_response(stop_download=...). The decisive difference is flow control. In Patch A, receive_data returns early after a StopDownload without acknowledging the frame's flow_controlled_length, so every stopped download leaks connection-level window; the independent test test_connection_usable_after_stop_download shows the consequence directly: after several stopped downloads on one HTTP/2 connection the next request times out (DownloadTimeoutError) under Patch A but passes under Patch B. That is exactly the production scenario the issue implies (a spider stopping downloads from bytes_received during a crawl), so Patch A leaves the feature unusable beyond a few requests per connection. Patch B explicitly calls acknowledge_received_data before stopping, uses ErrorCodes.CANCEL (the semantically correct code for a client-abandoned stream), and also guards window_updated against late WINDOW_UPDATE frames for streams already removed locally. On tests, both un-skip the shared crawler-based StopDownload tests, but Patch B additionally adds targeted tests for the END_STREAM edge cases, for connection reuse after a stop, and for the window_updated guard; Patch A adds none. On scope/craft, Patch B keeps crawler as an optional keyword argument so existing H2ConnectionPool/H2ClientFactory/H2ClientProtocol callers (including the existing protocol tests) keep working, whereas Patch A changes the positional settings parameter to crawler across three classes, which is unnecessary churn for the ask. Patch B also passes body_length=-1 for unknown length, consistent with the HTTP/1.1 handler, and adds a news entry. Patch A's only advantage is slightly less code, which does not offset the real correctness defect.

title: H2DownloadHandler: make acceptable server frame size configurable

judge.reasoning:
Both patches add a setting that is advertised to the server and both pass all seven independent tests, so the core ask is met by either. The differences are in robustness, edge handling and tests.

Correctness: Patch A builds the setting into the initial SETTINGS frame and also sets `conn.max_inbound_frame_size` directly, so larger frames are accepted immediately, independent of whether the server ever ACKs the client's settings. That matters for the issue's second use case (servers that ignore the advertised maximum, which are also the servers least likely to behave well). Patch B sends a second SETTINGS frame via `update_settings`; h2 only raises `max_inbound_frame_size` when the server ACKs, so acceptance of large frames depends on ACK ordering. In normal flows the ACK precedes response data, so B works in practice (the independent tests confirm), but it is strictly less robust. The issue explicitly names the standard's limits; A validates the range with a clear ValueError at handler init and in the protocol constructor, while B does no validation, so an out-of-range value surfaces as an h2 `InvalidSettingsValueError` thrown from `connectionMade` on every connection, which is a poor failure mode (logged by Twisted, requests likely hang). A's replacement of `conn.local_settings` reaches into h2 state more than B's use of the public `update_settings` API, but `local_settings`/`max_inbound_frame_size` are public attributes, A preserves the other defaults (and tests that), and the comment explains why.

Tests: A adds a focused in-memory h2 server suite that covers the default being advertised, a custom value being advertised with other settings preserved, rejection above the default, acceptance when configured, rejection above a custom value, both boundary values, and invalid values at both the protocol and handler level, including the exact 'server ignores the advertised maximum' scenario by forcing the server's outbound frame size. B adds one parametrized end-to-end test against the Twisted server; it would fail on base only on the final `local_settings.max_frame_size` assertion, never asserts that frames larger than 16384 were actually sent or received, and does not cover rejection, boundaries or invalid values.

Scope/craft: Both remove the known-limitation note and document the setting. B's docs add a useful caveat about DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE/WARNSIZE being per-frame and note that the httpx handler ignores the setting, and `HTTP2_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` arguably fits settings naming slightly better than `H2_MAX_FRAME_SIZE`; these are minor pluses for B. A's double validation (handler and protocol) is slight duplication but intentional fail-fast. On balance A resolves the issue more completely, handles the standard's limits the issue calls out, and backs it with far stronger tests.

issue_md:
The current implementation of HTTP/2 support in Scrapy requires servers to limit the [frame size](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7540#section-4.2) of the data that they send to the lowest maximum size that the standard defines, which is 16 384 bytes.

We should make this maximum configurable, at least within the limits that the standard defines (16 384 - 16 777 215), so that:

- The value can be fine-tuned for performance reasons.
- Scrapy can work with servers that ignore the maximum frame size indicated by Scrapy and send larger frames, which Scrapy does not allow (and should probably not allow, for security reasons).

title: HTTP cache should be for project but spider

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way: an opt-in setting that drops the spider-name partition from both built-in storages, and both pass every independent test. The difference is scope and test coverage. Patch A adds a single boolean HTTPCACHE_SHARED, touches exactly the two path/db-name computations, and its new tests live in the shared StorageTestMixin and DummyPolicyTestMixin, so they run against both FilesystemCacheStorage and DbmCacheStorage, cover the per-spider default, the shared case, isolation between shared and non-shared caches, and an end-to-end middleware hit with the 'cached' flag and httpcache/hit stat. Its only extra change is a harmless mkdir(exist_ok=True) cleanup. Patch B introduces a string enum HTTPCACHE_SCOPE and, beyond the issue's ask, a whole new 'domain' partitioning mode (hostname quoting, filesystem-only, with an IPv6 case that is skipped under a w3lib condition), plus an unrelated removal of the 'If empty, the HTTP cache will be disabled' sentence from HTTPCACHE_DIR docs. The value validation with a clear ValueError is a nice craft touch, and the enum is extensible, but the extra mode adds surface area and risk that the issue did not request, and B's tests stop at the storage layer with no middleware-level check. On correctness they are equal; on tests A is somewhat broader for the behaviour actually asked for; on scope A is clearly tighter. A is the better fix.

title: Support per-request download handler override

judge.reasoning:
Both patches resolve the issue: the independent tests pass on both, and each lets a request pick a handler different from its scheme handler without routing other requests through it. The difference is in design coherence and completeness.

Patch A integrates the feature into the existing handler machinery: a `DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS_BY_NAME` setting registers handlers under names, the `download_handler` meta key selects by name (or by an existing scheme), lookups reuse the same `_get_handler`/`_load_handler` path (so lazy/skip_lazy, NotConfigured memoization, old-style handler detection and `_close` all work unchanged), clashes between the two settings are rejected, and named handlers are explicitly kept from becoming downloadable URL schemes. It also handles a real consequence of the feature that B ignores: the default fingerprinter now distinguishes requests that differ only by handler, so a request routed to e.g. a browser handler is not dropped as a duplicate of the same URL fetched normally. Tests cover the clash, name-in-meta, scheme-in-meta, unknown ID, the scheme/name separation, fingerprint caching after meta mutation and the robots propagation. The robots.txt inheritance is a debatable policy choice, but it is documented with an escape hatch and does not break anything.

Patch B puts a class object or import path directly in request meta and builds a parallel subsystem: three new dicts (`_meta_handlers`, `_meta_notconfigured`, `_meta_old_style_handlers`), a copy of `_load_handler`'s try/except/warn block, a copy of the old-style dispatch in `_download_with_meta_handler`, instance-reuse-by-class heuristics spliced into `_load_handler`, and identity dedup in `_close`. That duplication is the kind that drifts. It also leaves dedup unaddressed, so two requests to one URL with different handlers collide in the dupefilter. B's tests are thorough for the module (reuse, close, NotConfigured, buggy, invalid path, end-to-end crawl), which is a genuine strength, but they test a more fragile design.

On correctness both fix the issue; A additionally handles the fingerprint interaction. On scope A's setting and fingerprint changes are larger but purposeful; B's extra reuse logic adds complexity without a clear need. On craft A is cleaner and consistent with the surrounding code. A wins.

issue_md: It would be great if a plugin like https://github.com/scrapy-plugins/scrapy-playwright did not had to force you to drive all requests through its download handlers, and instead you could drive certain requests through certain download handlers.

+.. _per-request-download-handlers:
+
+Using a different download handler for specific requests
+--------------------------------------------------------
+
+To download a specific request with a handler different from the one
+configured for its URL scheme, set the :reqmeta:`download_handler` request
+meta key:
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    yield scrapy.Request(
+        "https://example.com",
+        meta={"download_handler": "my.download_handlers.BrowserHandler"},
+    )
+
+The value can be a download handler class or its import path. The handler
+does not need to be listed in :setting:`DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS`. It is instantiated
+the first time that a request needs it, and that instance is reused for later
+requests. If a handler of the same class is already in use, e.g. because it is
+configured for some URL scheme in :setting:`DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS`, that instance
+is used instead.
+
+If the handler cannot be instantiated, e.g. because it raises
+:exc:`~scrapy.exceptions.NotConfigured`, the request is not downloaded and a
+:exc:`~scrapy.exceptions.NotSupported` exception is raised.
+

+a handler from :setting:`DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS` on a request whose URL uses a
+different scheme.

title: LinkExtractor calls process_value before applying allow and deny

judge.reasoning: The issue's stated expected behaviour is that allow/deny filter links before process_value is invoked. Patch A implements exactly that: when process_value is given, LxmlParserLinkExtractor builds a Link from the raw attribute value and runs the extractor's _link_allowed check before calling process_value, then still filters the processed result. It sensibly lets non-URL values (e.g. javascript: hrefs that process_value converts) through to process_value so the documented javascript example keeps working, only wires the filter when process_value is set (no cost otherwise), and updates the docstring to describe the new semantics. It adds meaningful tests covering each filter parameter, the javascript case, and the re-filtering of the returned value; the independent tests derived from the issue go from FAIL on base to PASS with A. Weaknesses of A: it is a behaviour change that can break users whose process_value rewrites a valid URL into one that only then matches allow (A's own test enshrines that this is now dropped), and it does a redundant safe_url_string/Link construction per link; these are real but modest risks. Patch B is docs-only, declaring the existing order intentional and pointing to Rule.process_links. The issue did allow for 'by design, but document it', so B is a defensible stance, but it leaves the reporter's actual expected behaviour unmet, adds no tests, and every independent test still fails under B. On correctness against the reported expectation and on tests, A is clearly ahead; its scope and craft are reasonable, so A wins.

I'm rather new to scrapy, created some 100 spiders and now moved the data to a MySql database.

"allow" and "deny" lists are ignored.

Tried on 2 test spiders with the same results.

I also could not find anything on web or in the issues here. Perhaps CrawlSpider/LinkExtractor/process_value seems not be used much...

title: Add possibility to use Selector (bytes) added in parsel 1.8.0.

judge.reasoning: Patch B does not actually achieve the issue's goal. It passes body/encoding to parsel, but the very next line still calls get_base_url(response), which on base reads response.text[0:4096] and thereby decodes and caches the entire body as a str. The independent tests confirm this: every 'does not use Response.text' and memory-peak test fails on B exactly as on base ('Response.text was used', retained decoded copy of the same size). So B's change is effectively a no-op for RAM. B also has correctness gaps: it feeds response.encoding directly to parsel, ignoring that TextResponse.text gives a BOM precedence over declared encodings, and it ignores the gb18030 custom error handler and utf-16/32 endianness defaults, so output can diverge from the previous .text-based behaviour. Beyond that, B bumps parsel/cssselect minimums and strips jmespath compat code and tests, which is unrelated churn with compatibility risk, and it adds no test that would fail before and pass after. Patch A addresses the root cause end to end: it builds the selector from bytes (gated on a parsel version that decodes in Python rather than truncating at bad bytes), and it adds _text_head so get_base_url/get_meta_refresh decode only the first few KB instead of the whole body, which is what makes the memory saving real. It mirrors TextResponse.text semantics (BOM precedence, utf-16/32 BE default, gb18030 and unknown-encoding fallbacks, cached-ubody reuse), keeps the root-ignored warning path, and ships substantive tests (forbid-text mocks, equivalence-with-.text parametrizations, head-decoding boundary cases, old-parsel fallback). Its skipif only triggers on old parsel, which is the fallback path by design. All independent tests pass on A and the encoding-correctness tests remain green. A is clearly the better fix.

issue_md:
## Summary

Please review possibility to apply RAM memory efficient Selector that can accept `bytes` as input 
added as result of https://github.com/scrapy/parsel/issues/210 (added in parsel 1.8.0) in scrapy (as default)

Currently UnifiedSelector (subclass of parsel's Selector used in scrapy) configured to use Response.text as input
Response.text (property) -> creates new object (Response.body -> converted to str) which is memory intensive and not needed 
https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/blob/5a37af146f4f036168ac562918fca43adb4ac65f/scrapy/selector/unified.py#L66-L73

## Motivation

As mentioned on https://github.com/scrapy/parsel/issues/210 usage of `str` input for creating Selector object is more RAM memory intensive

## Describe alternatives you've considered

At this stage it will require to.. separately create Selector object with bytes input inside spiders callback method (and not use Response.Selector)

## Additional context
Removing other usages of Response.text will significantly reduce RAM required to processing response

title: Investigate simplifying static checks for initialized Crawler

judge.reasoning:
Both patches reach the issue's goal: the late-initialized Crawler attributes become non-Optional for mypy and every `assert crawler.stats`-style narrowing is removed, and the independent static-type tests pass on both. They differ in how they get there.

Patch A replaces the attributes with a `_LateAttribute` descriptor that raises RuntimeError on read before the crawl starts. That is honest typing with runtime enforcement, but it is a public behavior change with real risk beyond the issue's ask: `crawler.engine`/`crawler.stats` went from returning None to raising, so any third-party `from_crawler` or pre-crawl code that reads them (even just to check `is None`) now crashes; worse, because the error is RuntimeError rather than AttributeError, `hasattr(crawler, 'stats')` and `getattr(crawler, 'stats', None)` also raise, which is a surprising trap. It also removes the attributes from the instance dict and adds ~50 lines of descriptor/overload machinery. A's new tests only exercise the new RuntimeError behavior and class-level access; none check the static types the issue is actually about.

Patch B keeps runtime behavior identical (attributes stay None until set) and just annotates them as non-Optional with `# type: ignore[assignment]`, documenting the arrangement in the class comment and the API docs. It is a type-level simplification exactly matching the issue's 'investigate simplifying static checks' framing, with zero runtime risk to Scrapy or third-party code. It also extends the treatment to `spider`, consistent with the issue's 'components such as'. Its runtime test is largely tautological against base, but its new `tests_typing/test_crawler.mypy-testing` file with `reveal_type` checks and an assert-free component sample is a direct regression test for the reported problem that would fail on base and pass after.

A's downside is the type lie it accepts, but the project already relies on documented lifecycle guarantees (and RuntimeError-raising getters like get_extension) for these attributes, so the lie is bounded and documented. Weighing correctness/risk, the more on-target tests, and scope, B is the better fix; A's broader redesign adds API breakage without being required by the issue.

issue_md: After we changed the Crawler logic to initialize components such as `Crawler.stats` later, static checkers (specifically mypy) don't know that when code like `self.crawler.stats.inc_value()` is called, `self.crawler.stats` is already initialized, so we need to add asserts in all methods that do this. We should try to find a way to do the same with fewer asserts. This also applies to 3rd-party code (middlewares etc.).

title: Improve open_in_browser function's handling of base tags in response.py

judge.reasoning: Both patches make every independent test pass, so the decision rests on robustness, scope, and tests. Patch A inserts the base tag after the real opening <head> if present, else after <html>, else after a doctype, else at the start (preserving a UTF-8 BOM), with HTML comments masked so commented-out <head>/<base> tags are ignored and offsets stay exact. It keeps the existing 'do not inject when a base tag already exists' behaviour, matches <base> case-insensitively without false-matching <basefont>, HTML-escapes the URL in the attribute, and skips injection for encodings like UTF-16 where ASCII bytes would corrupt the body. Its tests cover each fallback position, uppercase tags, newline-separated attributes, commented heads, basefont, escaping, BOM and UTF-16. Patch B takes a simpler route: always prepend a base tag (after a doctype only if the doctype is at the very start) and rely on the browser to hoist it into <head>. That works in browsers, but it changes semantics (a second base tag is always injected even when the response has one, with the existing test deleted and replaced), does not escape the URL, and only recognises a doctype at byte 0 (modulo whitespace), so a leading comment before the doctype would put <base> ahead of it and push the browser into quirks mode, which its own code comment says it wants to avoid. It also bumps the minimum w3lib requirement in pyproject.toml and tox.ini, an unexplained dependency change unrelated to the reported issue that adds risk for users, and it deletes the _remove_html_comments helper and its unit tests. Patch B's updated tests are reasonable but less thorough than A's. A resolves the issue more faithfully, with stronger tests and no unrelated churn.

issue_md:
The `open_in_browser` function in `response.py` uses a workaround to insert a `<base>` tag into the HTML response for local file viewing. As mentioned in the function's docstring, is "dirty" and could fail in situations where `<head>` tags are missing or improperly formed which can lead to unintended effects when rendering HTML.

Steps to Reproduce:
1. Use `open_in_browser` with an HTML response that does not contain a proper `<head>` tag.
2. Observe to see if the function does not handle this smoothly.

Edit the function to handle missing or properly formed `<head>` tags so that a correct `<base>` tag can be inserted.

title: Proposal: CLI improvements

judge.reasoning: The issue's concrete complaints are (1) `scrapy runspider spider3` with a name from `scrapy list` just says 'File not found' with no guidance, (2) crawl/runspider are not clearly distinguished in help/docs, and (3) running naively yields no stored output, which surprises users. Patch A addresses all three: `runspider` now detects when the argument is a project spider name (guarded by `inside_project()`, WARN_ONLY, and a broad except so the hint can never mask the original error) and tells the user to run `scrapy crawl <name>`; `crawl`, `check`, `fetch`, `shell`, and `parse` route unknown names through a shared `_load_spider` that raises a UsageError with a context-sensitive hint (use runspider for a file, `scrapy list` inside a project, 'no active project' otherwise) instead of a KeyError traceback; and both `crawl` and `runspider` gain `long_desc` text plus docs explaining that items are not stored unless `-o/-O` or FEEDS is used. The change to `crawl` (loading the class then passing it to `crawler_process.crawl`) is behaviour-preserving since `crawl()` already accepts a class. The `parse` change from log-and-continue to UsageError is a reasonable tightening. Patch A also adds a substantial test class covering unknown names across commands, the file-path-to-crawl hint, outside-project behaviour, the runspider-to-crawl hint, broken spider modules not hiding the error, over-long names, and help text content; these would fail on base and are not tautological. Patch B only reworded two `short_desc` strings and a few doc sentences; it adds no tests and leaves the actual error-message scenario from the issue unchanged (runspider still just says 'File not found'), and its docs edit oddly replaces the `crawl` line in the command list example with `runspider`. Independent tests confirm this: A passes all five, B fails the runspider-hint test and both help-text tests. A's extra scope (shared loader helper across commands) is in service of the same confusion the issue describes and adds little risk given the defensive guards. A is clearly the better fix.

issue_md:
## Summary

* Improve consistency in CLI arguments. 
* Modernize the usage.
* Possibly implement introduce a new, higher level command with its own sub-commands so as not to break existing code.

## Motivation

I find the CLI a little awkward and asymmetric: I'm always a little surprised about what's required to get expected results although I've used Scrapy for years.

Here's one example that I just experienced:

> Now, let me see what spiders are available.

```bash
$ scrapy list

spider1
spider2
spider3
```

> Ah hah. I want to run spider3. Let's see how to do it:


```bash
$ scrapy

Scrapy 2.13.3 - active project: my_project

Usage:
  scrapy <command> [options] [args]

Available commands:
  bench         Run quick benchmark test
  check         Check spider contracts
  crawl         Run a spider
  edit          Edit spider
  fetch         Fetch a URL using the Scrapy downloader
  genspider     Generate new spider using pre-defined templates
  list          List available spiders
  parse         Parse URL (using its spider) and print the results
  runspider     Run a self-contained spider (without creating a project)
  settings      Get settings values
  shell         Interactive scraping console
  startproject  Create new project
  version       Print Scrapy version
  view          Open URL in browser, as seen by Scrapy

Use "scrapy <command> -h" to see more info about a command
```

> Ok, **`runspider - Run a self-contained spider (without creating a project)`** rings a bell. 
And I definitely don't want to create a new project, so that sounds right.


```bash
$ scrapy runspider spider3

Usage
=====
  scrapy runspider [options] <spider_file>
scrapy: error: File not found: spider3
```

> Ok, I need to refer to it by filename...

```bash
$ scrapy runspider path/to/spider3
```

> Hmm. No output at the command line (stdout) nor to a file. (??) Let me look at the CLI help...

Etc. There are several other scenarios I can think of. Another is that `crawl` and `runspider` could be documented to more clearly distinguish them.



## Describe alternatives you've considered

Writing a wrapper script using a modern Python CLI library.


## Additional context

I've written a couple of dozen Scrapy Spiders, but these things still trip me up every time. Especially how running `crawl` or `runspider` naively with no options is basically a fail.

**Is there interest in a set of Issues to address various opportunities for improvements and PRs for them?**

title: scrapy settings --get does not account for add-ons

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported behaviour the same way at the core: in the settings command they call AddonManager.load_pre_crawler_settings, build a Crawler with the base Spider, and run crawler.addons.load_settings so both pre-crawler and update_settings changes are visible. All eight independent tests pass on both, so correctness on the issue's scenarios is equal.

Differences: Patch A copies the settings before mutating them, keeping the command's self.settings untouched, which is slightly cleaner than B mutating self.settings in place. A also applies the same pre-crawler loading to list/edit/genspider, which share the exact root cause (commands that never build a CrawlerProcess miss add-on changes such as SPIDER_MODULES); this is beyond the literal ask but low risk and directly tested, so it does not count against A. B instead adds a new --spider feature with docs; that is also out of scope and neutral on its own, but it is more product-surface than fix.

Tests tip the balance. A's new test class has a distinct name (TestSettingsCommandAddons) and covers get/getbool/getint/getfloat/getlist, pre-crawler settings, project and command-line priority. B names its new class TestSettingsCommand, which already exists earlier in tests/test_commands.py (visible in A's diff context, the base class ends right before TestCommandCrawlerProcess). Redefining it at module level shadows the original, so pytest would silently stop collecting the existing TestSettingsCommand tests, and ruff F811 would flag the redefinition. That is a concrete craft defect that quietly removes coverage. A's edit test has a win32 skip, which is a reasonable platform restriction and still runs on the POSIX hosts the issue's scenario would use (though I cannot verify its write_recording_editor helper exists, which slightly lowers confidence).

On balance A is the better patch: equivalent fix, cleaner handling of settings, tests that extend rather than clobber existing coverage.

issue_md: For example, if you run the `scrapy settings --get ZYTE_API_TRANSPARENT_MODE` command on a project whose `settings.py` file contains `ADDONS = {"scrapy_zyte_api.Addon": 100}`, you do not get `True`, even though the add-on [sets it](https://github.com/scrapy-plugins/scrapy-zyte-api/blob/5cfa54128235df25adacbdb05306c122eb1a9aef/scrapy_zyte_api/addon.py#L115).

title: Discourage using `CrawlSpider`

judge.reasoning: Patch A directly addresses the issue: it rewrites the CrawlSpider module docstring to drop the 'recommended spider' wording, adds a prominent note in docs/topics/spiders.rst saying CrawlSpider is not recommended for new code and that users should subclass Spider, adds a generic-spiders paragraph stating they are never required, discourages the `crawl` genspider template, and switches unrelated doc examples away from CrawlSpider to scrapy.Spider. It also adds a small test guarding the module docstring. The independent tests confirm it: both module-docstring tests fail on base and pass on A. Patch B never touches CrawlSpider at all; it is an unrelated refactor moving Spider attribute/method documentation into docstrings, adding type annotations, and dropping type-ignore comments. issue_md:
I've seen a lot of user questions about `CrawlSpider`, most of them caused by its limitations. I'm biased but when asked I awlays reply "please consider not using it". In my experience and opinion, the control flow in a `CrawlSpider` spider is both confusing by itself and too different from one in a normal spider that it should be only recommended for very basic spiders with no extensibility requirements.

We currently have this text from 2009 in [the CrawlSpider doc](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/latest/topics/spiders.html#crawlspider):

> This is the most commonly used spider for crawling regular websites, as it provides a convenient mechanism for following links by defining a set of rules. It may not be the best suited for your particular web sites or project, but it’s generic enough for several cases, so you can start from it and override it as needed for more custom functionality, or just implement your own spider.

As a minimally needed change, I think the first half shouldn't say anything like "the most commonly used" and the second half should more prominently say that you don't need to use `CrawlSpider` and you should switch to `Spider` if you run into limitations of `CrawlSpider`.

I will also agree with any of the more controversial suggestions, from adding "this isn't recommended to use for new code" and up to extracting it into a separate project or even deprecating and removing.

title: Deprecate the `download_delay` spider attr after refactoring AutoThrottle

judge.reasoning:
Both patches resolve the core ask: AutoThrottle stops writing `spider.download_delay` (each adds a downloader-level default delay that AutoThrottle overrides), and a user-defined `download_delay` attribute now triggers a ScrapyDeprecationWarning while still being honored. All four independent tests pass on both, so the decision rests on risk, scope, and craft.

Patch A is the conservative, focused fix. It keeps the existing precedence (spider attribute still overrides the setting, and AutoThrottle's start delay still replaces it, exactly as before), emits the warning in the same spot and style the base code already uses for `max_concurrent_requests`, adds a news entry under Deprecations, updates the settings/autothrottle/faq docs, and adds tests that cover the warning, the new `_default_slot_delay` precedence vs DOWNLOAD_SLOTS, the updated AutoThrottle unit tests, and an end-to-end mockserver crawl asserting the slot delay and that the spider attribute is no longer set.

Patch B takes a broader redesign: it deletes `_get_concurrency_delay`, bridges deprecated attributes into settings in `Crawler._apply_settings`, and makes the Downloader read only settings. That is architecturally tidy, but it carries extra risk and churn beyond the ask: (1) it changes precedence so that DOWNLOAD_DELAY set at spider or higher priority now silently wins over the attribute (previously the attribute always won), which is a behavior change folded into a deprecation step; (2) it remaps the already-deprecated `max_concurrent_requests` from CONCURRENT_REQUESTS to CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN and rewrites a historical release-notes entry to match, which is unrelated to this issue; (3) it reads the attribute from `spidercls` when `_apply_settings` runs before spider creation, so instance-level attributes set in a spider `__init__` can be missed in flows that apply settings early, whereas the base read the instance at slot-creation time; (4) it adds no news entry for the new deprecation, removes the settings.rst note while leaving the `spider-download_delay-attribute` label dangling, and rewrites the FAQ example to DOWNLOAD_SLOTS (unrelated churn). B's tests are reasonable (bridge applied/ignored, downloader `_delay`), but it drops the AutoThrottle test matrix that covered the spider attribute as the min delay and adds no integration test.

On correctness both work; on tests A is somewhat stronger (end-to-end coverage, keeps attribute-vs-setting matrix); on scope A is tighter while B's extra changes add real risk; on craft A includes the news entry and consistent doc updates. A is the better patch.

We deprecated almost all spider attrs used instead of settings, but `download_delay` is used to set the delay calculated by `AutoThrottle` so it can't be deprecated right now, but it would be nice to do that when it's possible.

title: Add Request.to_curl() method as the inverse of Request.from_curl()

judge.reasoning: Both patches add an identical core implementation: a `Request.to_curl()` method that lazily imports and delegates to `scrapy.utils.request.request_to_curl`, with the same circular-import workaround, and both register the method in the request-response docs. Independent tests pass identically on both. The differences are in tests and documentation. Patch B's tests are stronger: `test_to_curl` checks concrete output fragments (method/URL prefix, `--data-raw`, `-H`, `--cookie`) in addition to equality with the helper, and `test_to_curl_from_curl_roundtrip` directly verifies the 'inverse of from_curl' property the issue title asks for. Patch A's base-class test is purely tautological (`r.to_curl() == request_to_curl(r)`), and its only substantive test is a single POST-with-body string comparison in `test_utils_request.py`. On craft, Patch B's docstring is more informative (lists what is included and notes that downloader-middleware changes are not reflected, which is useful for the issue's stated debugging use case) and it adds a release-notes entry; its extra `autofunction` for `request_to_curl` is adjacent but harmless scope. Patch A's `versionadded:: VERSION` placeholder is ignored per the rules. No correctness difference, but B wins on test quality and documentation.

issue_md:
## Summary

Add a `to_curl()` method to `scrapy.Request` that turns the request into a curl cmd

## Motivation

`Request.from_curl()` already exists, but to go the other way you have to use a separate function, `scrapy.utils.request.request_to_curl()` (added in 2.9 #5892)

When I'm debugging a spider with `inspect_response()`, I often want to run a request outside Scrapy — from the terminal or in tools like Postman. Today I have to remember the import path to use it, I forget it often enough that I end up looking it up in the source:

```python
>>> from scrapy.utils.request import request_to_curl
>>> print(request_to_curl(request))
```

With a `to_curl()` method this is easier to find and matches `from_curl()`:

```python
>>> print(request.to_curl())
```

title: BaseSettings.update() does not accept iterable key-value pairs

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the identical functional change: extend the _SettingsInput alias with Iterable[tuple[str, Any]] and branch on hasattr(values, 'items') so non-mapping iterables are consumed directly as pairs. Both preserve the BaseSettings per-key-priority path and the JSON-string path, and the independent tests confirm both resolve every scenario (lists, tuples of two-item lists, generators, repeated keys, priority handling, Settings subclass). So correctness is a wash and the difference lies in tests and craft.

Tests: Patch A is noticeably stronger. It un-xfails the existing test and makes it assert both an overwrite and a new key with default priority, adds a priority test using a plain iterator (not just a list) that checks a higher-priority existing value is not overridden, and adds tests for setdict() and the BaseSettings/Settings constructors taking iterables, which are real entry points that delegate to update() and are now typed as accepting iterables. Patch B un-xfails the single test and adds a value + priority assertion, which is adequate but minimal and only exercises a list.

Craft: Patch B's single-loop structure with an `items` variable is slightly tidier than A's duplicated loop body, and B correctly narrows the stale 'doesn't support all inputs' comment to the remaining kwargs gap, whereas A leaves that comment unchanged (still technically true, just less precise). On the other hand, A's docstring explicitly explains the new iterable form and references dict.update, while B only tweaks the :type: line. These craft points roughly cancel.

Scope is equivalent for both. Given tests rank above craft and A's tests cover more of the surface the type change actually opens up, A is the better patch by a modest margin.

issue_md:
`BaseSettings` inherits from `MutableMapping`, but `BaseSettings.update()` does not accept iterable key-value pairs like `dict.update()` does.

### Example:

```python
from scrapy.settings import BaseSettings

settings = BaseSettings({"KEY": 0})
settings.update([("KEY", 1)])
```

title: Move internal scrapy.utils modules to internal names

judge.reasoning: The issue's remaining undeprecated modules (given base already has _compression, _versions, _shell and ignores for benchserver/console/gz/job/ssl/versions) are datatypes, display, ftp, ossignal, sitemap and template. Patch B deprecates all six, moving each to an underscored module, updating every internal call site (headers, resolver, misc, media, shell, fetch, files, etc.) and the shims emit ScrapyDeprecationWarning. Patch A omits datatypes entirely, leaving one of the issue's listed modules untouched; the independent test for scrapy.utils.datatypes deprecation fails on A and passes on B, and the patch text confirms A has no datatypes change. On tests, B adds tests/test_utils_deprecated_modules.py, which verifies each shim warns, re-exports the exact names, and that Scrapy's own modules never import the deprecated paths in a fresh subprocess; these would fail before and pass after. A only retargets existing test imports and adds no coverage for the deprecation behaviour. B also sweeps news.rst cross-references to literals so the docs build won't reference deprecated modules, which is consistent with the issue's 'not mentioned in the docs' criterion. Craft nits: B's new underscore imports are placed out of isort order in several files (e.g. _ossignal after misc, _ftp after defer), which A gets right, and A's rename to _colorize with a public tty_supports_color is a reasonable touch. Those are minor compared to A's missing module and lack of tests. B is the better fix.

issue_md:
Follow-up to https://github.com/scrapy/scrapy/pull/7007#discussion_r2775510982

Idea: I assume that most of (especially older) utils were moved there to organize the Scrapy code, not to allow users to use those functions. Even if we currently don't plan to remove or break them it's useful to be able to freely do that in the future.

For the first pass the criteria are:

* looking not at specific functions/classes but at whole modules;
* a module must not have names mentioned in the docs;
* deprecated names are ignored as if they don't exist;
* undocumented names that are definitely used by e.g. scrapy-poet or 3rd-party code that I could find or look like they may be useful to other users are for now treated as to be kept. 

This list is already huge:

  1. `benchserver`
     - *class* `Root`
  2. `console`
     - `get_shell_embed_func`
     - `start_python_console`
     - *const* `DEFAULT_PYTHON_SHELLS`
  3. `datatypes`
     - *class* `CaseInsensitiveDict`
     - *class* `LocalCache`
     - *class* `LocalWeakReferencedCache`
     - *class* `SequenceExclude`
  4. `display`
     - `pformat`
     - `pprint`
  5. `ftp`
     - `ftp_makedirs_cwd`
     - `ftp_store_file`
  6. `gz`
     - `gunzip`
     - `gzip_magic_number`
  7. `job`
     - `job_dir`
  8. `ossignal`
     - `install_shutdown_handlers`
  9. `sitemap`
     - `sitemap_urls_from_robots`
     - *class* `Sitemap`
  10. `ssl`
      - `get_openssl_version`
  11. `template`
      - `render_templatefile`
      - `string_camelcase`
      - *const* `CAMELCASE_INVALID_CHARS`
  12. `versions`
      - `get_versions`

I propose deprecating all of these, moving to underscored utils modules or next to call sites for utils that didn't prove to be worth a shared utils location.
